Detective Checklist

Keep this open while you investigate

If it's an image, look for…

  • Hands, fingers, and teeth: wrong counts or melted shapes
  • Text and signs in the background: garbled or nonsense letters
  • Lighting and shadows that point in different directions
  • Backgrounds that blur, warp, or repeat in strange ways
  • Skin, fur, or surfaces that look too smooth and perfect
  • Glasses, earrings, and patterns that don't match side to side

If it's writing, look for…

  • Vague sources: "experts say," "studies show." But who?
  • No specific names, dates, or places
  • Every sentence has the same shape and rhythm
  • Sounds smooth and confident but says very little
  • Facts stated confidently that turn out to be wrong

Then verify with SIFT

  • Stop: don't share or believe it yet
  • Investigate the source: who made this, and why?
  • Find better coverage: do trusted outlets report it too?
  • Trace it back: find the original photo, study, or quote
A Media Literacy Detective Game

Authentic or AI?

Twenty headlines, passages, and images. Some are completely real. Some were made by AI. Your class must decide, explain the clues, and back it up with evidence, because a guess is not enough for a detective.

Difficulty
Teams (optional)

Teacher tip: print the Student Evidence Sheet first (use Print Materials, top right) so students can write as you play. Keyboard: → advance · C checklist

Choose Your Case File

Pick any card, or press → to take them in order. Completed cards get a check.

Card 1
1 · Examine 2 · Think & Write 3 · Vote 4 · Reveal

Case Closed, Detectives!

You examined the evidence, explained your clues, and checked your sources. That is exactly what great media detectives do every day.

Exit Ticket

Which clue from today will you use most in real life, and why? Write 3–5 sentences. Include one example of something you might double-check this week (a post, a photo, a headline) and which SIFT move you'd use on it.
